notes.meaning: Eliphaz steps forward to begin the third round of speeches between Job and his friends. Being likely the oldest and most respected of the group, he speaks first each time. Instead of answering Job's actual points, he now turns to sharp and direct personal attacks.

Eliphaz asks whether a human being can add anything to God. He argues that God is completely self-sufficient, so even a person's wisdom helps only that person, not God. While it is true that God does not depend on us, Eliphaz wrongly implies that God does not care about our choices.

Eliphaz claims that human righteousness brings no special gain or added happiness to God. He thinks Job is acting as if God owes him a reward for good behavior. In reality, God does delight in upright people, but Eliphaz refuses to see that.

Eliphaz asks sarcastically if God is punishing Job because Job reveres Him. He also asks if God fears that Job might become too powerful. Since God does not discipline someone for doing good, Eliphaz assumes Job's suffering must be the punishment for great evil.

Eliphaz drops all polite hints and bluntly accuses Job of massive wickedness. He reasons backward: because Job suffers terrible pain, his sins must be endless. He offers no evidence at all, relying only on his own assumptions.

Eliphaz invents specific crimes to prove his point. He claims Job demanded unfair loan pledges from neighbors and took poor people's outer cloaks, leaving them with nothing to wear. Taking a poor person's only garment was a cruel form of oppression later condemned in Scripture.

Eliphaz accuses Job of refusing hospitality to traveling strangers and hungry people. In the desert lands, sharing water and food with travelers was a vital duty. Job had actually been generous, making this accusation completely baseless.

Eliphaz suggests that Job used his wealth and power to seize land for himself or favor other powerful people over the poor. He describes a man of influence who ruled the territory through raw power rather than fairness. Eliphaz paints Job as a tyrant who looked down on helpless neighbors.

Eliphaz charges Job with mistreating widows and orphans, the most defenseless people in ancient society. He says Job crushed their strength by taking away their support and refusing to help them. This was considered one of the worst social sins, though Job had actually spent his life defending the vulnerable.

Eliphaz explains Job's current misery as the direct payback for those supposed cruelties. He claims traps and sudden terror now surround Job because of how he treated others. In Eliphaz's mind, suffering is always the direct harvest of personal misdeeds.

Darkness and drowning waters are used here as pictures of deep disaster and overwhelming trouble. Eliphaz says Job is trapped in confusion and swallowed up by ruin. He believes these heavy disasters prove that God is executing justice against Job.

Eliphaz points to the night sky and the highest stars to show the immense majesty of God. God sits exalted far above the created universe in perfect holiness. Eliphaz brings this up to set up his next charge against Job's thinking.

Eliphaz falsely claims that Job acts as if God cannot see human affairs from so high up. He accuses Job of thinking that dark clouds hide the earth from God's judgment. Job never held or taught this, but Eliphaz twists Job's honest questions into blatant disbelief.

Eliphaz continues putting words into Job's mouth, claiming Job thinks God only walks about the heavenly dome and ignores the earth. In this view, God is too remote and unconcerned to care about human righteousness or wickedness. This was an ancient pagan idea about the gods, which Eliphaz wrongly pins on Job.

Eliphaz warns Job not to walk the old road of rebellion against God. He asks whether Job wants to adopt the mindset of corrupt generations from ancient times. He treats Job as someone who is in danger of following notorious sinners into ruin.

Eliphaz points back to ancient rebels who died suddenly before living out their natural lifespans. Their very homes and foundations were washed away by a rushing flood. Most commentators see this as a direct reference to the great flood in the days of Noah.

Those ancient wicked people told God to leave them alone, boasting that He could do nothing to help or harm them. Eliphaz uses the very words Job had earlier spoken about the wicked. But while Job used them to show that evil people sometimes thrive, Eliphaz uses them to insist that rebels are always wiped out.

Even though those wicked people defied God, God in His mercy had originally filled their homes with good things. Eliphaz quotes Job's own statement about rejecting the advice of the wicked, but he turns it against Job as a sarcastic jab. He implies that he is truly loyal to God, while Job is siding with evil men.

When God finally judges the wicked, godly people rejoice to see justice done and God's honor defended. The innocent can laugh at the fall of evil because arrogance has finally been defeated. Eliphaz suggests that Job's downfall is part of this very pattern.

The righteous celebrate that their oppressors are cut down and their leftover wealth is eaten up by fire. Many commentators see an allusion here to the fiery destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah. Eliphaz groups himself with the righteous survivors, implying Job belongs with the destroyed.

Eliphaz switches from fierce criticism to gentle urging, telling Job to get right with God and find peace. He promises that returning to the Lord will bring blessing and prosperity back into Job's life. The advice is true and beautiful in itself, though it wrongly treats Job as an enemy of God.

Eliphaz urges Job to listen to God's teaching and store His words deep inside his heart. He tells him to shape his thinking by divine revelation rather than bitter feelings. Treasuring God's word in the heart is a central biblical pattern for spiritual health.

Eliphaz promises that if Job repents and turns back to God, his ruined life will be rebuilt. He must purge any hidden sin and unfair gain from his home. While God truly restores those who turn to Him, Eliphaz wrongly assumes Job had turned away.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some popular modern teachers use this verse to claim that repenting and reforming your life guarantees physical and material wealth, but Scripture shows God does not promise immediate outward wealth to everyone who turns to Him.

notes.meaning: Eliphaz tells Job to stop valuing wealth and treat fine gold like common dust or gravel in a creek bed. The gold of Ophir was known as the finest gold of the ancient world. Eliphaz believes Job's true idol was money and that he must cast it aside.

When a person stops trusting in earthly riches, God Himself becomes their greatest treasure and defense. Having the Almighty is worth far more than stacks of pure silver. This is one of the highest and truest statements in the whole book of Job.

Eliphaz says that genuine fellowship with God brings deep joy and confidence. Instead of hanging his head in guilt or sorrow, Job would be able to look up to God with peace and gladness. Delighting in God is the true fruit of being reconciled to Him.

Eliphaz assures Job that once he repents, God will eagerly answer his prayers. Job would then thankfully carry out the vows, or sacred promises, he made when crying out for help. In a twist of irony, God later answered Job's prayer to save Eliphaz himself.

Eliphaz promises that Job's plans will succeed and clear divine guidance will brighten his path. Where Job currently sees only darkness, God's favor would provide success and clarity. Eliphaz ties all these earthly blessings directly to outward repentance.

Eliphaz describes how Job will become an effective intercessor, praying for others when they are brought down by trouble. God hears the prayers of the humble and rescues those who are cast low. A truly restored person uses their position to lift up those who are struggling.

In his closing sentence, Eliphaz states that God will spare even a guilty person because of Job's clean hands and pure prayers. Without realizing it, Eliphaz speaks a prophecy about himself. At the end of the book, Eliphaz and his friends are spared from God's wrath only when Job prays for them.
